To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the information content of musical notes modulated the amplitude of low frequency oscillatory activity in bilateral STG, right MTG and left insula from within 100, 200 and 300 ms of note onset, and high frequency oscillatory activity from 200 to 500 ms after note onset in these same areas.

low-frequency activity (theta to gamma) in the superior temporal, middle temporal and inferior frontal cortices, anterior cingulate cortex, and insula, is modulated by unexpectedness in the auditory domain, with the modulation of high frequency activity in the superior temporo-parietal cortices occurring after the modulation of low frequency activity.

the information theoretical predictability of music is reflected in the low- to high-frequency oscillatory power of the brain, with the information content of musical notes modulating the amplitude of low- to high- frequency oscillatory activity in bilateral superior temporal gyrus and right middle temporal gyrus from within 100 to 200 msec of musical note onset.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the information content of music modulates low-frequency oscillations (LFOs) in the STG and MTG and that LFOs in the STG are followed by high-frequency oscillations (HFOs), which are observed in the ACG and the insula.

we show that musical notes that are more surprising elicit stronger low-frequency activity in the STG and MTG and stronger high-frequency activity in the ACG, insula, and STG, and that this pattern of results holds across individuals.
the neural consequences of predictive processes are observable in a variety of neural oscillations in a variety of brain areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the information theoretic predictability of a musical note is reflected in the amplitude of low frequency oscillatory activity (0.5–30 Hz) within 500 msec of its onset in multiple cortical and subcortical regions.
prediction error signaling is a dynamic, multicomponent process that involves both cortical and subcortical regions and is observable in both low- and high-frequency oscillatory activity.
the time course of neural prediction error signaling is complex and involves a series of low- and high-frequency modulations in a wide range of cortical and subcortical regions.
